docs.title: What is zoetty?
docs.text:
zoetty turns terminal sessions into small, looping, animated clips made of plain SVG or HTML and CSS. No video, no GIF, no JavaScript.

~/my-project $ zoetty init clips/hello.toml✓ wrote clips/hello.toml next: zoetty build clips/hello.toml$ zoetty build clips/hello.toml✓ clips/hello.svg (4.2KB)$ zoetty check clips/hello.toml✓ clips/hello.toml$

That's zoetty, recorded by zoetty, and shown here as its HTML output: try selecting the text. Every clip in these docs is built from a spec in docs/clips/, and the test suite fails if any of them are out of date.

docs.title: Why use zoetty?
docs.text:
Terminal GIFs go stale, weigh megabytes, look blurry, and have to be re-recorded by hand every time the output changes.

  • Real output - zoetty record runs your commands in a real terminal and keeps their colours.
  • Small and sharp - A clip is a few KB of text, crisp at any size.
  • Works in READMEs - The SVG is just an image: it plays on GitHub, PyPI and anywhere else that shows one.
  • Or in your docs - The HTML fragment drops into any page, with selectable text.
  • Kept in your repo - The spec is a short TOML file. When your tool changes, re-record and rebuild.
  • Checked in CI - zoetty check fails if a clip is out of date.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Describe the clip in a TOML file: the commands to type, and where their output comes from.
  2. Record it: zoetty record runs the commands in a pseudo-terminal and saves what they print, colours and all, next to the spec.
  3. Build it: zoetty build renders the spec to an .svg, an .html fragment, or both.
  4. Check it in CI: zoetty check fails if a built clip no longer matches its spec.

Timing is generated, not recorded: commands are typed at a steady speed and output appears line by line, so clips never sit on a long pause or dump everything at once.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
uv tool install zoetty
zoetty init docs/clips/hello.toml    # write a starter spec
zoetty build docs/clips/hello.toml   # render it to docs/clips/hello.svg

Then put it in your README like any image:

![What the clip shows](docs/clips/hello.svg)

Next: the clip format, embedding clips and examples.

docs.title: Use it with your coding agent
docs.text:
Paste this into Claude Code, Codex, Cursor or similar:

Use zoetty to add an animated terminal demo of this project to the README.
Read https://phalt.github.io/zoetty/agents/ first and follow it: install zoetty,
write a clip spec in docs/clips/ that shows the most useful commands, record the
real output with `zoetty record`, build it with `zoetty build`, look at the result,
embed the SVG in README.md, and add `zoetty check docs/clips/*.toml` to CI.

See Using zoetty with an agent for what the agent will follow.

The first release.

  • zoetty init, record, build and check.
  • Clip specs in TOML: [[run]] sessions with recorded or hand-written output, or hand-timed [[step]]s.
  • zoetty record runs commands in a pseudo-terminal the size of the clip, keeps their colours, types input after each prompt and ends with Ctrl-D.
  • SVG output for READMEs and anywhere that takes images; HTML fragments for docs sites, safe to put several on one page.
  • Long output wraps at cols and scrolls past rows. [theme] colours, optional window chrome, and reduced-motion support.

docs.title: 🤖 Using zoetty with an agent
docs.text: zoetty works well with coding agents (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and others): a clip is a short text file, every command reports what it did, and zoetty check tells you when you're done.

docs.title: The prompt
docs.text:
Paste this into your agent, in the repo you want a demo for:

Use zoetty to add an animated terminal demo of this project to the README.
Read https://phalt.github.io/zoetty/agents/ first and follow it: install zoetty,
write a clip spec in docs/clips/ that shows the most useful commands, record the
real output with `zoetty record`, build it with `zoetty build`, look at the result,
embed the SVG in README.md, and add `zoetty check docs/clips/*.toml` to CI.

Change the first line to ask for something more specific: a clip for one docs page, a REPL session using a library, or replacing an old GIF.

docs.title: Instructions for agents
docs.text:
If you're an agent that's been sent here, follow these steps.

  1. Install zoetty with uv tool install zoetty (or pip install zoetty). Check with zoetty --version.
  2. Decide what the clip shows. One idea per clip, ideally 2 to 4 commands and under 25 lines of output. Read the project's README and docs to choose the commands a new user would run first.
  3. Write the spec in docs/clips/<name>.toml. Start from zoetty init docs/clips/<name>.toml or the examples. Every key is in the clip format. In particular:
    • Write a label that says what happens in the clip, in a sentence. It's the alt text.
    • Give each command an output file under docs/clips/captures/, so its real output is recorded. Only use lines for output you can't record.
    • Set cols to fit the widest output line (usually 72 to 100), and rows if there's more output than fits comfortably.
    • Use [record] setup to reset anything a command creates (rm -rf my_output), so recording again gives the same clip.
    • Use exec when the command needs a path or prefix the reader shouldn't see (.venv/bin/tool, uv run tool, cd example &&).
    • Use input for anything that prompts or for a REPL. It's sent after the program goes quiet, then Ctrl-D.
  4. Record it: zoetty record docs/clips/<name>.toml. Read the output: every run should be ✓, or ! if the command is meant to fail. Open the capture files and check they hold what you expected. Never edit captures by hand: fix the spec or the setup and record again.
  5. Build it: zoetty build docs/clips/<name>.toml.
  6. Look at it. Open the SVG in a browser, or take screenshots at a few points if you can. Check nothing is cut off at the right edge (raise cols), nothing important scrolls away too fast (raise rows or line_gap), and the timing feels natural.
  7. Embed it.
    • README: ![<label>](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/<owner>/<repo>/main/docs/clips/<name>.svg). A full URL works on GitHub and PyPI.
    • Docs sites: the SVG as an image, or add .html to out and include the fragment. See embedding.
  8. Keep it fresh. Add zoetty check docs/clips/*.toml to CI (e.g. uvx zoetty check docs/clips/*.toml). Commit the spec, captures and built files together.

docs.title: Don'ts
docs.text:
• Don't write output by hand that you could record: the point is that the clip shows what the tool really does.
  • Don't put secrets, tokens or personal paths in specs or captures. Check the capture files before committing.
  • Don't record commands that change things outside the repo (deploys, publishing, sending messages).

docs.title: Updating clips later
docs.text:
When a tool's output changes, the same agent can refresh every clip:

The output of this project's CLI has changed. Re-record and rebuild the zoetty
clips in docs/clips/ (zoetty record, then zoetty build), look at each one, and
make sure `zoetty check docs/clips/*.toml` passes.

docs.title: 📟 Command line
docs.text: Every command takes one or more spec files, so a shell glob does a whole folder: zoetty build docs/clips/*.toml.

docs.title: zoetty init SPEC
docs.text:
Writes a starter spec to SPEC, which builds as it is. It won't overwrite a file that already exists.

zoetty init docs/clips/hello.toml

docs.title: zoetty record SPEC...
docs.text:
For each spec: runs its [record] setup commands, then every run that has an output file (and isn't record = false), in order, in a pseudo-terminal the size of the clip. What each command prints is saved to its output file.

zoetty record docs/clips/start-api.toml

docs/clips/start-api.toml
  ✓ clientele start-api -f schema.json -o my_client/ · exit 0 → docs/clips/captures/start-api.ansi
  ✓ ls my_client/ · exit 0 → docs/clips/captures/ls.ansi

A command that exits non-zero is marked ! and still recorded. A failing setup command or a timeout stops that clip and makes record exit 1.

Runs with lines are never executed, so record is safe to run on every clip.

docs.title: zoetty build SPEC...
docs.text:
Renders each spec to its out files.

zoetty build docs/clips/*.toml

✓ docs/clips/hello.svg (4.3KB)
✓ docs/clips/hello.html (4.0KB)

If a spec is broken, or a run's output hasn't been recorded yet, build says so, carries on with the others, and exits 1.

docs.title: zoetty check SPEC...
docs.text:
Checks each spec is valid and that every one of its out files exists and matches a fresh build. Nothing is written. Exits 1 if anything is wrong, so it's made for CI:

zoetty check docs/clips/*.toml

✓ docs/clips/hello.toml
✗ docs/clips/zen.svg is out of date: run zoetty build docs/clips/zen.toml

check doesn't re-record anything: it trusts the captures in your repo. It only needs zoetty installed, not the tools your clips show.

docs.title: zoetty --version
docs.text: Prints the version.

docs.title: 📜 Clip format
docs.text:
A clip is described by a TOML file, usually kept in docs/clips/. Paths in it are relative to the file.

The smallest clip has a label and one run:

label = "Listing the files in a project"

[[run]]
cmd = "ls"
lines = ["README.md  src  tests"]

zoetty build turns clip.toml into clip.svg next to it.

docs.title: Top-level keys
docs.text: Key Default What it does label required What the clip shows, in words. Used as the alt text and aria-label, so people who can't see the animation still get it. title "" Shown in the window bar, like a terminal's title. cols 80 Terminal width in columns. Recording uses it too, so output wraps where it would in a real terminal of that size. rows every line Visible rows. Output scrolls once it passes this. out ["<name>.svg"] Files zoetty build writes. .svg makes an SVG image, .html an HTML fragment. prompt "[dim]$[/] " Shown before each command. final_prompt prompt Left blinking at the end. typing_speed 28 Characters per second commands are typed at. Typing always takes between 0.4 and 2.2 seconds. line_gap 0.07 Seconds between output lines. hold 4.0 Seconds the last frame is held before the clip loops. duration worked out Total loop length in seconds, if you'd rather set it. chrome true Draw the window bar with its dots and title.

docs.title: [[run]]: commands
docs.text:
Each run is a command typed at the prompt, followed by its output. Runs are shown in order.

[[run]]
cmd = "clientele start-api -f schema.json -o my_client/"
output = "captures/start-api.ansi"
Key Default What it does cmd required The command typed on screen. output A file holding the command's captured output. zoetty record writes it. lines Output written by hand, one markup string per line. exec cmd What zoetty record actually runs, when it's different from what's shown (e.g. .venv/bin/tool instead of tool, or cd demo && tool). input Text typed into the command while recording. Each line is typed once the command has been quiet for a moment, so it lands after the prompt that asked for it. Then Ctrl-D is sent, which ends a REPL. record true Set to false to keep an output file but never re-record it. prompt the clip's A different prompt for this command, e.g. ">>> " inside a REPL. think 0.5 Seconds between finishing typing and the output appearing. pause 0.9 Seconds after the output before the next command. line_gap the clip's Seconds between this run's output lines.

A run has output or lines, not both. A run with neither shows no output.

Output lines wider than cols wrap onto the next row, as they would in a terminal.

docs.title: [record]: how commands are recorded
docs.text:
[record]
cwd = "../.."                       # run from the repo root
setup = ["rm -rf my_client"]        # run first, output not shown
env = { NO_COLOR = "" }
timeout = 120
Key Default What it does cwd the spec's folder Where commands run. setup [] Shell commands run before the first recorded command, to start from a known state. Recording stops if one fails. env {} Extra environment variables. timeout 60 Seconds each command may take.

Commands also get TERM=xterm-256color, COLUMNS and LINES from the clip's size, FORCE_COLOR=1 and CLICOLOR_FORCE=1 so they keep their colours, and PAGER=cat and GIT_PAGER=cat so nothing waits on a pager. env can override any of them.

A command that exits non-zero is recorded like any other (failing commands make good demos too); zoetty record shows its exit code.

docs.title: [theme]: colours
docs.text:
[theme]
bg = "#282c34"
bar = "#21252b"
fg = "#abb2bf"
green = "#98c379"

bg, fg (text), bar (window bar) and the six colours blue, green, yellow, red, cyan and magenta, as #rgb or #rrggbb. Anything you don't set keeps its default.

docs.title: Markup
docs.text:
lines, prompt and final_prompt use a small markup, a lot like rich's:

Markup Shows [bold]text[/] Styled text. Styles are bold, dim, italic, and the colours blue, green, yellow, red, cyan and magenta. [bold green]text[/] Several styles at once. \[ A literal [. In TOML strings write \\[, or use single-quoted strings: '\[y/N]'. [type 1.2]text[/] Text typed out over 1.2 seconds. [type 1.2 0.5] waits 0.5 seconds first. Only needed in [[step]] clips: commands in runs are typed for you.

Captured output is converted to markup automatically: colours and bold, dim and italic are kept; cursor movement and other escape codes are dropped.

docs.title: [[step]]: hand-timed clips
docs.text:
For clips that aren't a series of commands, give [[step]] entries instead of [[run]]s, saying exactly when lines appear. A clip has runs or steps, not both.

label = "A prompt being answered"
duration = 6

[[step]]
at = 0.5
lines = ['Start? \[y/N] [type 0.1 0.8]y[/]']
caret = true

[[step]]
at = 2
lines = ["[green]✓ started[/]"]
Key Default What it does at required Seconds into the clip the lines appear. lines required Markup lines. caret false Show a blinking caret at the end of the last line, until the next step.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• zoetty reads output line by line rather than emulating a terminal. Colours are kept and a carriage return keeps what was last written on the line (so simple spinners end up showing their final state), but full-screen programs and progress bars that move the cursor won't look right.
  • Wide characters such as emoji take one column in zoetty's layout but two in most terminals, so text after them can sit slightly off.

docs.title: 🖼️ Embedding clips
docs.text:
One spec can build both formats:

out = ["demo.svg", "demo.html"]
SVG HTML fragment Use it in READMEs, PyPI, anything that shows images Docs sites and pages you control How ![alt](demo.svg) or <img> Paste or include the file's contents Text Part of the image Real text people can select and copy Fonts The viewer's monospace font The page's, or a monospace font you load Size A few KB A few KB

Both loop for ever, fade out before restarting, and show the finished screen with no animation for people who prefer reduced motion.

docs.title: SVG in a README
docs.text:
GitHub strips <style> from README HTML, so an HTML clip won't animate there. An SVG referenced as an image does, because its animation is CSS inside the SVG file:

![zoetty building a clip](docs/clips/demo.svg)

PyPI shows your README too, but it can't follow relative paths. Use the file's full URL on GitHub so the clip works in both places:

![zoetty building a clip](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/you/project/main/docs/clips/demo.svg)

The image is served from main, so it updates when you merge, and a README on an old PyPI release shows the latest clip.

Inside an image, an SVG can't load web fonts, so it uses the viewer's monospace font. zoetty pins every run of text to its column, so the layout holds whichever font that is.

docs.title: HTML in a docs site
docs.text:
The .html file is a fragment: a <div> and a <style>, with no <html> or <body>. Every class and animation name starts with the file's name (zt-demo-...), so several clips can share a page.

With MkDocs, include it with the snippets extension:

# mkdocs.yml
markdown_extensions:
  - pymdownx.snippets:
      base_path: ["docs"]

--8<-- "clips/demo.html"

This page's examples are embedded exactly like that. Anything else that lets you put raw HTML in a page works the same way: Hugo shortcodes, Jekyll includes, Astro components, or plain copy and paste.

docs.title: Matching your site's colours
docs.text:
Set [theme] to your site's code colours, so a clip sits next to your code blocks as if it belonged there:

[theme]
bg = "#282c34"
bar = "#21252b"
fg = "#abb2bf"

docs.title: Keeping clips fresh
docs.text:
Commit the spec, the captures and the built files. When the tool a clip shows changes:

zoetty record docs/clips/*.toml
zoetty build docs/clips/*.toml
git diff docs/clips/

And in CI, so a clip can't silently go stale:

- name: Check terminal clips are up to date
  run: uvx zoetty check docs/clips/*.toml

docs.title: 🎞️ Examples
docs.text: Every example here is a real spec from docs/clips/, built by zoetty. Some are shown as their SVG and some as their HTML fragment: the HTML ones have text you can select.

docs.title: Hello: output written by hand
docs.text:
The smallest useful clip. Nothing is recorded: each run's lines say what it printed, using markup for colour.

# The smallest useful clip: two commands, with their output written by hand.
title = "~/my-project"
label = "Typing two commands in a terminal: echo prints a greeting, ls lists three files"
cols = 60
out = ["hello.svg", "hello.html"]

[[run]]
cmd = "echo 'Hello from zoetty!'"
lines = ["Hello from zoetty!"]

[[run]]
cmd = "ls"
lines = ["[blue]docs[/]  README.md  [green]tool.py[/]"]

As an SVG:

And the same spec as an HTML fragment:

~/my-project $ echo 'Hello from zoetty!'Hello from zoetty!$ lsdocs README.md tool.py$

docs.title: Quick start: recording real output
docs.text:
zoetty recording itself. Each run has an output file, so zoetty record runs it for real and keeps its colours. [record] runs the commands in a scratch folder, and setup empties it first, so the clip is the same every time it's recorded. exec is what actually runs; cmd is what's shown.

# zoetty recording itself: init a clip, build it, check it.
title = "~/my-project"
label = "zoetty init writes a starter clip spec, zoetty build renders it to SVG, and zoetty check confirms it is up to date"
cols = 72
out = ["quickstart.svg", "quickstart.html"]

[record]
cwd = "/tmp"
setup = ["rm -rf zoetty-quickstart", "mkdir zoetty-quickstart"]

[[run]]
cmd = "zoetty init clips/hello.toml"
exec = "cd zoetty-quickstart && zoetty init clips/hello.toml"
output = "captures/quickstart-init.ansi"

[[run]]
cmd = "zoetty build clips/hello.toml"
exec = "cd zoetty-quickstart && zoetty build clips/hello.toml"
output = "captures/quickstart-build.ansi"

[[run]]
cmd = "zoetty check clips/hello.toml"
exec = "cd zoetty-quickstart && zoetty check clips/hello.toml"
output = "captures/quickstart-check.ansi"
~/my-project $ zoetty init clips/hello.toml✓ wrote clips/hello.toml next: zoetty build clips/hello.toml$ zoetty build clips/hello.toml✓ clips/hello.svg (4.2KB)$ zoetty check clips/hello.toml✓ clips/hello.toml$

docs.title: A REPL: typing into an interactive program
docs.text:
input is typed into the program while it's recorded, one line each time it goes quiet, so every line lands after the prompt that asked for it. After the last line zoetty sends Ctrl-D, which ends the REPL and brings back the shell prompt. env turns on Python's plain REPL, which doesn't redraw the line as you type.

# An interactive program: `input` is typed into it while recording,
# one line each time it goes quiet, so answers land after their prompts.
title = "python"
label = "A Python REPL importing zoetty's markup parser and parsing some styled text"
cols = 64
out = ["repl.svg", "repl.html"]

[record]
env = { PYTHON_BASIC_REPL = "1" }

[[run]]
cmd = "python -q"
output = "captures/repl.ansi"
input = """
from zoetty.markup import parse, plain
plain(parse("[bold]zoe[/]tty"))
[s.styles for s in parse("[bold green]ok[/] done")]
"""
pause = 0.2

docs.title: Scrolling and themes
docs.text:
rows sets how much of the terminal is visible: past that, output scrolls up line by line. line_gap slows the output down so it can be read, and [theme] recolours the window, here to One Dark.

# Long output scrolls once it passes `rows`, and [theme] recolours the window.
title = "python -m this"
label = "python -m this printing the Zen of Python, scrolling past the bottom of a ten-row terminal"
cols = 72
rows = 10
line_gap = 0.18
hold = 3
out = ["zen.svg", "zen.html"]

[[run]]
cmd = "python -m this"
output = "captures/zen.ansi"

[theme]
bg = "#282c34"
bar = "#21252b"
fg = "#abb2bf"
blue = "#61afef"
green = "#98c379"
yellow = "#e5c07b"
red = "#e06c75"
cyan = "#56b6c2"
magenta = "#c678dd"
python -m this $ python -m thisThe Zen of Python, by Tim Peters Beautiful is better than ugly.Explicit is better than implicit.Simple is better than complex.Complex is better than complicated.Flat is better than nested.Sparse is better than dense.Readability counts.Special cases aren't special enough to break the rules.Although practicality beats purity.Errors should never pass silently.Unless explicitly silenced.In the face of ambiguity, refuse the temptation to guess.There should be one-- and preferably only one --obvious way to do it.Although that way may not be obvious at first unless you're Dutch.Now is better than never.Although never is often better than *right* now.If the implementation is hard to explain, it's a bad idea.If the implementation is easy to explain, it may be a good idea.Namespaces are one honking great idea -- let's do more of those!$

docs.title: Hand-timed steps
docs.text:
For clips that aren't a series of commands, [[step]] entries say exactly when each line appears and [type ...] types text out. This one re-enacts a paulrun session and is the clip on paulrun's README.

# A hand-timed clip: [[step]] entries say exactly when each line appears.
# This is the clip on the paulrun README, re-enacting `paulrun hello.md`.
title = "~/hello"
label = "paulrun checking and running hello.md: it asks for NAME, shows the plan, runs a shell step and a Python step, and finishes ok"
duration = 16
out = ["steps.svg", "steps.html"]
cols = 56

[[step]]
at = 0.4
caret = true
lines = ["[dim]$[/] [type 1.3]paulrun check hello.md[/]"]

[[step]]
at = 2.2
lines = ["[green]hello.md: ok[/]"]

[[step]]
at = 2.8
caret = true
lines = ["[dim]$[/] [type 0.9]paulrun hello.md[/]"]

[[step]]
at = 4.2
caret = true
lines = ["NAME [dim](Who to say hello to)[/]: [type 0.5 0.4]Paul[/]"]

[[step]]
at = 5.5
lines = [
  "[blue]╭─ [/][bold blue]Say hello[/][blue] ─────────────────────╮[/]",
  "[blue]│[/] [dim]directory[/]  /home/you/hello      [blue]│[/]",
  "[blue]│[/] [dim]inputs[/]     NAME=Paul            [blue]│[/]",
  "[blue]│[/] [dim]steps[/]      1. Greet             [blue]│[/]",
  "[blue]│[/]            2. Count the letters [blue]│[/]",
  "[blue]│[/] [dim]blocks[/]     2 run blocks         [blue]│[/]",
  "[blue]╰─────────────────────────────────╯[/]",
]

[[step]]
at = 6.1
caret = true
lines = ["Start? \\[y/N] [type 0.05 0.8]y[/]"]

[[step]]
at = 7.4
lines = ["", "[bold blue]1/2  Greet[/] [blue]━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━[/]"]

[[step]]
at = 7.7
lines = ["  [dim italic]Saying hello to Paul.[/]"]

[[step]]
at = 8.0
lines = ["", "  [dim]┌ [/][bold]sh[/][dim] · 10:02:13.482[/]"]

[[step]]
at = 8.4
lines = ["  [dim]│[/] Hello, Paul!"]

[[step]]
at = 8.7
lines = ["  [dim]└ [/][green]✓ exit 0[/][dim] · 0.0s[/]"]

[[step]]
at = 9.2
lines = [
  "",
  "[bold blue]2/2  Count the letters[/] [blue]━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━[/]",
  "",
  "  [dim]┌ [/][bold]python[/][dim] · 10:02:13.483[/]",
]

[[step]]
at = 9.9
lines = ["  [dim]│[/] Paul has 4 letters"]

[[step]]
at = 10.2
lines = ["  [dim]└ [/][green]✓ exit 0[/][dim] · 0.1s[/]"]

[[step]]
at = 10.8
lines = [
  "",
  "[green]╭──────────────────────╮[/]",
  "[green]│ ✓ [/][bold]finished ok[/][dim] · 0.1s[/][green] │[/]",
  "[green]╰──────────────────────╯[/]",
]

[[step]]
at = 11.5
caret = true
lines = ["[dim]$[/] "]

docs.title: 🚀 Install
docs.text:
zoetty is a command-line tool, so install it on its own rather than into a project:

uv tool install zoetty

Or with pip:

pip install zoetty

Check it worked:

zoetty --version

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Python 3.12 or later
  • macOS or Linux. zoetty record needs a pseudo-terminal, which Windows doesn't have. zoetty build and zoetty check only read and write files, but are only tested on macOS and Linux.

docs.title: In CI
docs.text:
To check clips in CI you only need zoetty itself, not the tools the clips record:

- name: Check terminal clips are up to date
  run: uvx zoetty check docs/clips/*.toml
